newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: W. Australia on track for 6.4 mln tonne wheat crop.
newsitem.headline: W. Australia on track for 6.4 mln tonne wheat crop.

text.p: Western Australia is on track to produce 6.4 million tonnes of wheat in 1997/98, private forecaster Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd said on Monday.

Moreover, given a longer growing season this year, there is a possibility of matching the 7.42 million tonnes recorded last year, the group said. The higher crop yield would depend on whether spring rains arrive at or before some of the critical stages of crop development, it said.
AWF's forecast for total Australian wheat crop for 1997/98 (April-March) was lifted slightly to 17.87 million tonnes from the 17.85 million forecast made last month.

The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) has forecast a 1997/98 Australian wheat crop of 16.25 million tonnes, while the Australian Wheat Board expects a crop of around 18 million tonnes.
"Western Australia is quite safe from a crop failure," Australian Wheat Forecasters said.
In Queensland, a major high protein-producing state, stored subsoil moisture is above average, it said.
However, crops need rain to allow the surface roots to grow and link up with moisture deeper down the soil horizon, the group said.
Better structured Darling Downs soils are more likely to keep crops growing longer than shallower soils in other areas, Australian Wheat Forecasters said.
A similar situation exists for northern New South Wales, it said.
"Immediate concerns for crops faded when a rain of between 25 and 40 millimetres was received by both the central west and Riverina regions," Australian Wheat Forecasters said.
Crops in Victoria, except for the Western Mallee, have consolidated well and appear strong and healthy, it said.

The impact of a possible El Nino-related drought in Australia is more likely to impact negatively on wheat crops to be sown in the 1998/99 season than on the current crop, Australian Wheat Forecasters said.
